docs.title: Network Sandbox Engine (NSE)
docs.text: Deterministic Linux network namespace isolation and kernel nftables trace evaluation engine.

docs.title: What is NSE?
docs.text:
Network Sandbox Engine (NSE) is a Python library and CLI tool designed for testing, verifying, and debugging Linux nftables firewall rulesets inside ephemeral network namespaces (netns).

NSE allows security engineers, tool developers, and CI/CD pipelines to validate complex network filtering rulesets without touching the host firewall or requiring dedicated VMs. The ruleset under test is loaded only inside the sandbox namespaces. A run does create temporary namespaces, the host end of its veth links with their addresses (or, with isolated_host=True, a namespace of its own for that end), gateway routes to the sandbox subnets, and ownership records under /run/nse. Each is journalled before it is created and removed at teardown, or by recovery after a crash.

graph TD
    subgraph Step1["1. Test Specification"]
        Req["<b>TestRequest</b><br/>ruleset + packets + topology"]
    end

    subgraph Step2["2. Ephemeral Netns Sandbox"]
        direction TB
        Netns["<b>Netns Setup</b><br/>nse_<id> & veth links"]
        RuleEng["<b>Rule Engine</b><br/>validate & load nftables"]
        Inject["<b>Scapy Injector</b><br/>L2/L3 packet injection"]
        NFT["<b>Kernel nftables</b><br/>meta nftrace set 1"]

        Netns --> RuleEng
        RuleEng --> Inject
        Inject --> NFT
    end

    subgraph Step3["3. Trace Evaluation & Oracle"]
        direction TB
        Harvester["<b>Trace Harvester</b><br/>nft monitor trace stream"]
        Oracle["<b>Deterministic Oracle</b><br/>TraceEvents & verdicts"]

        Harvester --> Oracle
    end

    Step1 --> Step2
    Step2 --> Step3

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Library and CLI only: no server, no socket, no daemon. Root privileges are held for the duration of a run and nothing listens.
  • Self-verifying Oracle: canary packets before and after every run prove the kernel trace was actually being observed, so a blind engine fails instead of reporting a clean result.
  • Wire-level Leak Assertions: PCAPAsserter captures on a named interface, so a test can assert a stimulus produced no frame at all - the question nft monitor trace cannot answer.
  • Isolated Topologies: Supports Simple (single sandbox netns) and Gateway (router + server netns chain) topologies.
  • Scapy Packet Injection: Forge arbitrary TCP, UDP, and ICMP packets across IPv4 and IPv6 protocols.
  • Ownership-aware Lifecycle: every namespace, link and route is journalled before it is created. Teardown and crash recovery remove only what a run can prove it owns, and stop every process still in a sandbox namespace.
  • Managed Processes: real servers and clients in the sandbox, with a verified UID, GID and capabilities, timeouts, and output limits.
  • Reproducible Reports: an experiment report and a SHA-256 manifest that let a CI artifact reconstruct a run.
  • Worked Examples, run in CI: workstation, IPv6, coexisting tables, NAT gateway, a real application, and two experiments that must fail; see Worked Examples.
  • Full Type Safety & Strict Lints: Built with Pydantic v2, mypy --strict, import-linter, and ruff.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
import asyncio
from nse.core.netns_controller import NetnsController
from nse.core.pipeline import run_test_pipeline
from nse.models.test_request import TestRequest, PacketSpec

rules = """
table ip filter {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;
        tcp dport 80 accept
    }
}
"""

request = TestRequest(
    rules=rules,
    packets=[
        PacketSpec(protocol="tcp", src_ip="10.0.0.1", dst_ip="10.0.0.2", dst_port=80),
        PacketSpec(protocol="tcp", src_ip="10.0.0.1", dst_ip="10.0.0.2", dst_port=22),
    ],
)

async def main():
    controller = NetnsController()
    events = await run_test_pipeline(request=request, controller=controller)
    for evt in events:
        if evt.verdict:
            print(f"Packet verdict: {evt.verdict}")

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Explanation: Architecture
docs.text: NSE is a library and a CLI. There is no server, no socket, and no daemon: you call it, it builds a namespace, measures, and tears the namespace down.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
graph TD
    CLI["nse.cli.runner<br/>YAML suites, exit codes"] --> Core
    Lib["Your code<br/>run_test_pipeline()"] --> Core

    subgraph Core["nse.core"]
        Pipeline["pipeline<br/>orchestration + canary probes"]
        Netns["netns_controller<br/>namespaces, veth, topologies"]
        Rules["rule_engine<br/>nft --check, nft -f"]
        Inject["scapy_injector<br/>L2/L3 forging"]
        Harvest["trace_harvester<br/>nft monitor trace parsing"]
    end

    Core --> Models["nse.models<br/>TestRequest, PacketSpec, TraceEvent"]
    Core --> Kernel["Linux kernel<br/>netns + nftables + netlink"]

import-linter enforces two boundaries in make lint:

  • nse.core and nse.models must not import nse.cli — the engine cannot depend on the CLI that drives it;
  • nse.models must not import the engine — models stay a leaf.

docs.title: Privilege model
docs.text:
NSE runs as root, because creating network namespaces, loading nftables rulesets and reading kernel trace events all require it.

It holds those privileges only for the duration of a run, and it exposes no network or IPC surface while it does. That is a deliberate change:

Version Model 1.1.0 – 1.1.1 An unprivileged FastAPI server delegating to an nse-rootd daemon over a UNIX socket. 2.0.0 The FastAPI server ran in-process as root. Fewer moving parts, considerably more attack surface. 2.1.0 onward No server at all. The web interface is archived; NSE is a library and a CLI.

Removing the web layer removed the reason to have a long-lived root process, and with it the JavaScript toolchain, the ASGI stack, and a CI job. For a tool whose job is to be trusted about firewall behaviour, a smaller audited surface is worth more than a GUI.

The code for the web interface remains in git history at tag v2.0.0.

docs.title: Isolation guarantee
docs.text:
Rulesets are only ever loaded inside nse_<id> / nsr_<id> / nss_<id> namespaces. RuleEngine.load() refuses an empty namespace name outright, so a missing argument cannot fall through to the host firewall. Teardown removes both the namespaces and the host-side veth interfaces, with a retry backoff, and a startup recovery removes only verified abandoned resources whose owner lock is available. Unmarked, replaced or uncertain resources are preserved with a diagnostic; see namespace lifecycle.

The host firewall is not modified, but by default it is on the path from the sandbox to the host end of the link. That traffic is local input for the host. NSE warns when an input hook may filter it, and create_namespace(..., isolated_host=True) moves that end into a namespace of its own; see the host endpoint.

docs.title: Explanation: The Verdict Oracle
docs.text: NSE decides pass/drop outcomes from kernel nftables trace events. This page is about the part that matters more than the parsing: how NSE knows it was looking.

docs.title: The problem this solves
docs.text:
A firewall test is a negative assertion — "this packet did not get through". Negative assertions have a failure mode that positive ones do not: if the instrument stops working, the assertion still holds. A trace monitor that never attached to the kernel produces exactly the same output as a firewall that blocked everything.

Up to 2.0.0, NSE had that failure mode in three places at once:

  • the readiness probe signalled when the read loop was scheduled, not when nft monitor trace had subscribed to the kernel;
  • the trace deadline was fixed when the loop started, so a long packet sequence outlived it and the verdict stream was truncated with no error;
  • the CLI runner treated a mismatch between expected and observed verdict counts as something to print, not something to fail on.

Together, a completely blind run exited 0.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
Every run carries its own positive control.

graph LR
    A["Load ruleset<br/>+ nse_trace scaffolding"] --> B["Start<br/>nft monitor trace"]
    B --> C{"Readiness canary<br/>observed?"}
    C -->|no, after N retries| X["ORACLE ERROR<br/>run reports nothing"]
    C -->|yes| D["Inject test packets<br/>(deadline extended per packet)"]
    D --> E{"Liveness canary<br/>observed?"}
    E -->|no| X
    E -->|yes| F{"Read loop ended cleanly?<br/>Every line parsed?"}
    F -->|no| X
    F -->|yes| G["Verdict stream<br/>(canaries removed by trace id)"]
  1. Trace scaffolding: RuleEngine.load() prepends a table inet nse_trace prerouting chain with meta nftrace set 1, so every packet entering the namespace produces trace events.
  2. Readiness canary: a probe packet is injected and re-injected until its own kernel trace event is observed. This is a proof, not a signal: nothing proceeds until the kernel has demonstrably delivered an event.
  3. Sequential injection: test packets go in one at a time, and the trace deadline is pushed forward after each one. The read loop polls its deadline, so an extension takes effect even while it is parked on a read.
  4. Liveness canary: a second probe after the last test packet. If it is not observed, the monitor stopped watching part-way through and the verdict stream is truncated by an unknown amount.
  5. Health check: the harvester's terminal state must be a clean stop — not an unexpected EOF, a timeout or a crash — and its count of unparsed trace lines must be zero.
  6. Reporting: canary trace ids are removed from the results, so probes never appear in your verdict stream. A canary counts as observed only when a trace matching the canary's packet tuple arrives, so unrelated traffic in the namespace cannot vouch for the oracle.

Any failure in steps 2, 4 or 5 emits an error event. The CLI runner fails on error events, and reports them as oracle errors, kept separate from firewall failures in the summary: a broken measurement and a broken ruleset are different problems and want different fixes.

docs.title: Verdict reduction
docs.text:
reduce_verdicts() collapses a trace stream into one verdict per packet:

  • events are grouped by trace_id — one packet's traversal of the netfilter stack shares an id across chains;
  • events from the nse_trace scaffolding table are excluded, since they exist only to switch tracing on;
  • only stimulus traces are counted. The pipeline attributes each trace from the addresses, protocol and ports of its first hook, which runs before any user NAT chain, and records them on every event as packet_src_ip, packet_dst_ip, packet_protocol, packet_src_port, packet_dst_port and packet_role (stimulus, response or background). Later hooks inherit the first role, so translated addresses cannot change it. A server reply, such as the gateway listener's UDP answer being dropped on the way back, is a response; spontaneous traffic, such as IPv6 neighbour discovery, is background. Both stay in the event stream for diagnosis, but neither adds a verdict. The exact count check is unchanged, so a missing or duplicated stimulus is still an oracle error;
  • DROP and REJECT beat ACCEPT, because a packet accepted by one chain and dropped by another did not get through;
  • a trace id that reached the user ruleset but produced no verdict is omitted. That makes the observed count differ from the expected count, which is an oracle error — deliberately, rather than being rounded up to a pass.

REJECT is indistinguishable from DROP in the reduced stream, so an expectation of REJECT is compared as DROP.

docs.title: What the contract proves, and what it does not
docs.text:
The canary, parser and liveness checks are NSE's strongest guarantee, and the reason a clean result can be trusted. Each is a positive control on the instrument itself:

Check Proves Readiness canary The monitor delivers kernel events for packets on the injection path before the stimuli. Liveness canary It still delivers them after the last stimulus: the stream is not truncated. Parser health Every trace line was understood: a format change cannot hide verdicts. Read-loop health The monitor ended cleanly, not by EOF, timeout or crash. Count check (CLI) One verdict per expected stimulus, no more and no fewer.

They prove that the trace oracle observed the path the canaries took. They say nothing about a capture. PCAPAsserter readiness means its socket is armed and filtering on one interface. It does not mean that the traffic you care about crosses that interface.

An empty capture is evidence of "nothing left" only next to a positive control that shows the same capture seeing the stimulus. Without one, it is no evidence at all. examples/broken_observer.py runs both failure modes, a blind oracle and a capture on the wrong interface, and shows each being caught for its own reason. The experiment report keeps these questions apart:

  • result.oracle and outcome describe the trace oracle;
  • each attached CaptureReport describes a capture;
  • caller-declared PositiveControl entries describe the evidence for the assertion.

docs.title: Proving the contract holds
docs.text:
The guarantee above is itself tested. Setting NSE_FORCE_BLIND=1 makes the parser understand nothing — which is what a kernel trace format change looks like from the outside — and make test-blind asserts that the suite then fails. That job runs in CI on every push.

Separately, test_parser_understands_every_line_of_a_real_trace asserts, against whatever kernel the runner has, that a real run left zero trace lines unparsed. CI runs it on more than one image so a format change breaks a build rather than silently blinding the oracle.

docs.title: Explanation: Namespace Lifecycle & Naming Conventions
docs.text: Each controller owns the resources it creates. A new controller can recover a previous run's abandoned resources, but cannot delete another live controller's resources merely because their names have an NSE prefix.

docs.title: Names identify a family, not ownership
docs.text:
The pipeline derives names from its test ID:

Component Pattern Example Simple namespace nse_<test_id> nse_a1b2c3d4e5f6 Router namespace nsr_<test_id> nsr_a1b2c3d4e5f6 Server namespace nss_<test_id> nss_a1b2c3d4e5f6 Isolated host endpoint (create_namespace(..., isolated_host=True)) nsh_<name> nsh_nse_app Host veth vhr-<suffix> vhr-3f9a0c41b2e Peer veth (simple netns) / router host veth vrh-<suffix> vrh-3f9a0c41b2e Router server veth vrs-<suffix> vrs-3f9a0c41b2e Server veth vsr-<suffix> vsr-3f9a0c41b2e

<suffix> is the first 11 hex characters of a BLAKE2s digest of the whole test ID (or of the namespace name for create_namespace()), so every name fits Linux's 15 byte limit and IDs sharing a prefix no longer collide. Before v2.2.0 the suffix was the first 8 characters of the ID, and the simple topology's in-namespace peer was always called veth-nse; that fixed name was created in the host namespace first, so two concurrent runs collided on it.

Migrating rules that matched veth-nse

Since v2.2.0 the simple topology's in-namespace interface is vrh-<suffix>, not veth-nse, and this is the permanent name. Rules inside the sandbox that match iifname "veth-nse" / oifname "veth-nse" should match the prefix instead (iifname "vrh-*") or use the exact name from derive_names(test_id).veth_router_host.

Before any mutation, setup checks that the interface names are free and that the requested subnets do not overlap a route already present on the host (including another run's connected or gateway routes). A conflict fails with OwnershipError and leaves the kernel untouched. Concurrent topologies need distinct subnets: pass them through TestRequest.network (SimpleNetwork/GatewayNetwork) or the YAML network: key. The defaults are unchanged for single runs. Gateway host routes are derived from the configured server subnets and recorded as owned resources; pre-existing routes are never replaced or removed.

create_namespace(name) continues to expose its interface names through sandbox.ext_iface and sandbox.peer_iface. With isolated_host=True the host end lives in nsh_<name> (sandbox.ext_netns) instead of the host namespace. It is reserved, recorded and removed together with the sandbox, and the route overlap check does not apply to it; see the host endpoint. Neither these conventions nor prefixes authorize deletion. Network address/name conflicts between otherwise independent topologies still need compatible configuration.

docs.title: Private ownership journals
docs.text:
Creating a controller does not create network resources. Its first mutation opens a private lease and writes a versioned journal under /run/nse/netns-<device>-<inode>/, scoped to the calling thread's network namespace. The runtime directory is mode 0700; journal and lock files are mode 0600, owned by the caller (root for real network operations).

Each controller has a random owner ID. Separate namespaces/experiments within the controller have distinct run IDs; the router and server of one gateway share a run ID. Each resource also has a fresh random token. The journal records namespace identities, veth endpoints and locations, and host routes tied to their owning link. PID, process start time and boot ID are diagnostics and scope checks; a PID is never the activity test.

Every creation intent is written before the kernel operation. Updates use a temporary file, flush/fsync, atomic replacement and directory fsync. A journal is limited to 4 MiB; exceeding that limit refuses the next mutation before its kernel operation. Symlinks, hard links, non-regular files, unexpected owners, public permissions, unsupported schemas and inconsistent identities are rejected. Journals contain resource data, not recovery commands to execute.

Keep the controller alive while using its resources. Its owner lock remains held even between operations; normal cleanup does not release the controller for reuse by a different owner. After the controller is discarded or its process dies, startup recovery can acquire that lease and check the resources.

docs.title: Kernel identity checks
docs.text:
Namespace ownership combines the named namespace's device/inode identity with a marker on its loopback interface. Veth endpoints carry a marker containing owner ID, run ID and resource token in their interface alias. The lookup checks the recorded namespace identity before entering it. A matching resource found under a renamed interface can still be removed by its marker; a different resource reusing its old name is preserved.

Some kernels ignore interface aliases supplied during veth creation. NSE therefore assigns both endpoints fresh, locally administered unicast MACs in the creation request, then applies the aliases explicitly. For a pending creation interrupted before alias confirmation, recovery requires both generated MACs and the mutual veth peer relationship in the recorded creation namespace. One address or one name alone is insufficient. Once creation is confirmed, the alias marker is required; the temporary MAC check cannot bypass a missing or altered marker on a completed resource.

docs.title: Coordinated cleanup and recovery
docs.text:
startup_sweep() keeps its existing signature. Under a coordination lock shared by all NSE controllers in that runtime scope, it:

  1. Finds ownership journals and tries to acquire each owner lock without waiting.
  2. Leaves live owners alone, including other controllers in the same process.
  3. Validates an inactive owner's metadata and checks the actual kernel resources.
  4. Removes verified links first, then namespace names. Routes attached to a deleted link disappear with it; unrelated routes are never explicitly deleted.
  5. Persists unresolved entries for another attempt, removing the journal and its owner lock file only when all entries have been discharged.

The same coordination lock covers ordinary creation, journal changes and teardown, preventing competing recoverers or new instances from racing through an NSE mutation. These are cooperative locks: unrelated privileged tools do not participate in them.

destroy_netns(name) now deletes only a namespace recorded by that controller and still carrying the recorded identity/marker, along with its owned links. cleanup_all() uses the same checks for all of that controller's resources. Namespace deletion is retried up to three times, with 100 ms and 500 ms waits between attempts. Failed deletion retains ownership and emits a warning; cleanup_all() can retry it. Unresolved links keep their namespace recorded.

The method signatures and return types are unchanged. Consumers that used destroy_netns() to remove a namespace created externally must manage that external resource themselves.

docs.title: Forks, processes and conservative recovery
docs.text: Lease descriptors are close-on-exec. After os.fork(), NSE closes the child's inherited registry descriptors without unlocking the parent's shared file description. An inherited controller cannot mutate ownership state: create a new controller in the child. Reusing a controller from a different network namespace is also rejected.

docs.title: Processes and the namespace boundary
docs.text:
Removing a namespace name alone would not stop the processes inside it: they would keep the namespace alive, unnamed and unreachable. So before NSE deletes a namespace, at teardown or during crash recovery, it stops every process whose network namespace is that one: SIGTERM, a grace period, then SIGKILL. This covers processes NSE started, anything they left behind (even detached with setsid), and anything else running there.

  • Membership is checked through a pidfd: a PID that was recycled after it was listed is never signalled. Recovery therefore needs no record of PIDs; the namespace itself is the record.
  • Refusal: NSE's own network namespace and PID 1's are never swept.
  • Outside the boundary: a process that moved itself to another network namespace, which requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN.

Managed processes (start_process()) are additionally stopped as a process group, with a verified identity; see managed processes.

Resources without sufficient proof stay untouched, with warnings:

  • Legacy prefix matches from versions without journals require manual review.
  • A crash between successful namespace creation and application of its first loopback marker leaves a recorded, unconfirmed intent. It cannot safely be distinguished from a reused name, so automatic recovery preserves it.
  • Missing/corrupt metadata, changed markers, unavailable namespace locations or exhausted deletion retries preserve the unresolved entries.

Do not remove a journal to force deletion: it removes ownership evidence. Review the journal and current kernel resources, then clean up only confirmed abandoned objects. A running version 2.1.2 still has its old prefix sweep and can delete resources belonging to 2.2.0; upgrade cooperating instances before running them concurrently.

The regression suite exercises real traffic in two processes, normal teardown, SIGKILL, recovery before veth alias application, unregistered prefix matches, reused names, corrupt records, concurrent recoverers and fork inheritance.

For the underlying lock and namespace semantics, see flock(2) and ip-netns(8).

docs.title: How-To: Proving a Capture Saw the Whole Window (Beacons)
docs.text:
A capture's report can show that the kernel dropped nothing, but not that the capture was reading the right link when it mattered. A sniffer that attached late, or that watches an interface the traffic no longer crosses, produces a clean, complete, empty window. That reads exactly like "nothing left".

A beacon closes that gap. It is a small Ethernet frame sent at a known moment on a known link. A capture that sees a beacon before a window and another after it was demonstrably reading across the window.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
from nse import PCAPAsserter

capture = PCAPAsserter(iface=ns.ext_iface, netns=ns.ext_netns)
await capture.start()
await capture.mark("start")                 # on the captured interface itself
# ... the stimuli under test ...
await capture.mark("from-sandbox", via=ns)  # from the sandbox's end of the link
packets = await capture.stop()
report = await capture.stop_report()

assert report.beacons_missing == [], report.beacons_missing
assert report.window_complete is True, report

mark() sends the frame and records it as expected. The report then lists:

  • beacons_expected: every beacon sent for this capture;
  • beacons_seen: every beacon frame the capture read, with its time and position among the frames;
  • beacons_missing: the labels of expected beacons that were not seen.

A missing beacon makes the window incomplete: window_complete is False. Every tool that reads that property, such as observe() and correlate(), then refuses to turn an absence into False.

Beacon frames count in packets_observed and are written to the PCAP file, but they are never in the list stop() returns, so they never match a stimulus.

docs.title: Where the frame comes from
docs.text:
Call Sent from Proves capture.mark(label) the captured interface, in the capture's namespace the capture was reading at that moment capture.mark(label, via=sandbox) sandbox.peer_iface, inside the sandbox that, and that the sandbox's link reaches the capture beacon = await sandbox.beacon(label) then capture.expect(beacon) the sandbox, at a moment of your choice the same as via=

expect() accepts any beacon, for instance one sent before a step that may renumber or recreate the link.

docs.title: What a beacon is
docs.text:
The frame is an Ethernet broadcast with EtherType 0x88B5 (IEEE 802 local experimental): never routed, and never IP. No IP firewall rule touches it, so seeing it says nothing about the rules under test, only about the instrument. Its payload is NSE-BEACON, a version byte, a 16-byte random token and the label (up to 64 bytes of UTF-8). The token, not the label, identifies it.

Sending needs CAP_NET_RAW in the sending namespace, as capturing does. The frame is sent from a thread created for the purpose, which enters that namespace and ends with it.

docs.title: Filters, and when mark() refuses
docs.text:
NSE's default capture filter admits beacons. A custom filter= may not, and a beacon the filter drops would make every window incomplete. So mark() raises CaptureStateError on a capture with a custom filter unless it was created with beacons=True. That flag ORs ether proto 0x88b5 into the filter:

capture = PCAPAsserter(iface=ns.ext_iface, filter="udp port 53", beacons=True)
# effective filter: ((<default>) and (udp port 53)) or (ether proto 0x88b5)

mark() also refuses on a capture that is not running, and on a link without an Ethernet header (a tun device, for example), where the frame cannot exist.

NSE's own tests check the blind case explicitly. A beacon sent through a filter that excludes it, or on a link the capture does not watch, comes out as beacons_missing and window_complete is False.

docs.title: Snaplen and link type
docs.text:
The report also says what the capture could physically see:

Field Meaning hardware_type the interface's Linux ARPHRD_* type link_type the PCAP LINKTYPE_* of the frames (1: Ethernet, 101: raw IP), or None when unknown snaplen the most bytes of one frame the capture reads packets_truncated frames read at exactly snaplen bytes, so possibly cut short required_bytes what you declared you need, with PCAPAsserter(required_bytes=...) snaplen_sufficient required_bytes <= snaplen; None when nothing was declared

If you declare required_bytes and the snaplen is smaller, window_complete is False: an assertion about bytes the capture cannot hold must not pass on what it truncated.

docs.title: How-To: CI/CD Pipeline Setup
docs.text: Integrate NSE into GitHub Actions or GitLab CI to automatically test firewall rulesets on every commit.

docs.title: GitHub Actions Workflow
docs.text:
Create .github/workflows/ci.yml:

name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'
      - run: make setup
      - run: make lint

  unit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'
      - run: make setup
      - run: make test

  integration:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'
      - run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y nftables iproute2 conntrack
      - run: make setup
      - run: |
          sudo .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/ -v -m "integration"
          sudo .venv/bin/nse-runner --file tests/test_suite.yaml --report-dir nse-report
      # Keep the evidence, especially when the suite fails.
      - if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: nse-report
          path: nse-report/

The nse-report artifact holds report.json and manifest.json (see CLI reference). From it you can reconstruct each case:

  • the request and its ruleset, with hashes;
  • the NSE, Python, dependency, kernel and tool versions;
  • every trace event, the canary checks, and the verified identity of the listeners;
  • the outcome, and what teardown left behind.

Isolate the experiment from the runner's network

Some hosted runners route part of 10.0.0.0/24, NSE's default subnet, to their own interface, and NSE refuses to build a topology that would shadow a host route. Run the privileged steps in an empty network namespace, as NSE's own CI does: sudo unshare --net -- sh -c 'ip link set lo up; exec .venv/bin/nse-runner --file tests/test_suite.yaml --report-dir nse-report'. Alternatively, give the cases an explicit network:.

docs.title: Local CI Verification (make ci-local)
docs.text:
Run the unprivileged part of the pipeline locally before pushing - lint, type checks, import boundaries, unit tests, the docs build and the release artifacts:

make ci-local

It is not the whole of CI. Three jobs are deliberately left out because they need privileges or the network that a pre-push hook should not assume: integration (root, real namespaces), blindness (make test-blind, which proves the runner fails when the parser understands nothing) and smoke-pypi. Run sudo make integration-test and make test-blind when you have touched the harvester, the oracle or the CLI exit codes.

docs.title: How-To: Custom Packet Specifications
docs.text: NSE allows forging custom TCP, UDP, and ICMP packets across IPv4 and IPv6 protocols using PacketSpec.

docs.title: PacketSpec Schema
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal

class PacketSpec(BaseModel):
    protocol: Literal["tcp", "udp", "icmp"] = Field(description="Layer 4 protocol")
    src_ip: str = Field(default="10.0.0.1", description="Source IPv4 or IPv6 address")
    dst_ip: str = Field(default="10.0.0.2", description="Destination IPv4 or IPv6 address")
    src_port: int | None = Field(default=12345, description="Source port for TCP/UDP")
    dst_port: int | None = Field(default=80, description="Destination port for TCP/UDP")
    tcp_flags: list[str] | None = Field(default=None, description="TCP flags, e.g. ['SYN', 'ACK']")

docs.title: TCP Flags & State Testing
docs.text:
Forge TCP packets with specific flags:

# SYN Packet
syn_packet = PacketSpec(
    protocol="tcp",
    src_ip="10.0.0.1",
    dst_ip="10.0.0.2",
    dst_port=443,
    tcp_flags=["SYN"]
)

# ACK Packet
ack_packet = PacketSpec(
    protocol="tcp",
    src_ip="10.0.0.1",
    dst_ip="10.0.0.2",
    dst_port=443,
    tcp_flags=["ACK"]
)

docs.title: IPv6 Packets
docs.text:
Specify IPv6 addresses for automatic IPv6 / ICMPv6 injection:

ipv6_packet = PacketSpec(
    protocol="icmp",
    src_ip="fd00:1::1",
    dst_ip="fd00:2::2",
)

docs.title: How-To: Embedding NSE in Python
docs.text: NSE is a library first. This guide covers calling the engine directly from your own test suite, which is how you assert things about a ruleset that a YAML file cannot express.

docs.title: Running one test
docs.text:
import asyncio

from nse.core.netns_controller import NetnsController
from nse.core.pipeline import run_test_pipeline
from nse.models.test_request import PacketSpec, TestRequest

RULES = """
table ip filter {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;
        tcp dport 80 accept
    }
}
"""

async def main() -> None:
    request = TestRequest(
        rules=RULES,
        packets=[
            PacketSpec(protocol="tcp", dst_port=80),
            PacketSpec(protocol="tcp", dst_port=22),
        ],
    )
    events = await run_test_pipeline(request=request, controller=NetnsController())

    # ALWAYS check for oracle errors before reading verdicts.
    errors = [e.raw_message for e in events if e.type == "error"]
    if errors:
        raise AssertionError(f"the measurement failed, not the firewall: {errors}")

    for evt in events:
        if evt.verdict and evt.table != "nse_trace":
            print(f"[{evt.chain}] {evt.verdict}")

asyncio.run(main())

Check for error events first

run_test_pipeline returns an error event when its canary probes were not observed, i.e. when the kernel trace was not actually being read. If you skip that check and go straight to counting verdicts, an empty list looks exactly like "the firewall dropped everything" — which is the bug this whole design exists to prevent. Reuse nse.cli.runner.collect_oracle_errors if you like.

docs.title: Reducing a trace stream to verdicts
docs.text:
Rather than filtering events by hand, reuse the runner's logic:

from nse.cli.runner import collect_oracle_errors, reduce_verdicts

errors = collect_oracle_errors(events)
assert not errors, errors

assert reduce_verdicts(events) == ["ACCEPT", "DROP"]

reduce_verdicts groups events by trace_id, drops NSE's own nse_trace scaffolding, and resolves each packet to a single verdict with DROP/REJECT taking precedence over ACCEPT.

docs.title: The experiment report
docs.text:
run_test_pipeline_report() runs the same experiment as run_test_pipeline(). Instead of the event list it returns an ExperimentReport, from which a CI artifact alone is enough to reconstruct the run:

from nse.core.pipeline import run_test_pipeline_report

report = await run_test_pipeline_report(request, controller=controller, timeout=60)

report.result.outcome            # "completed", "rules_invalid", "setup_failure",
                                 # "instrument_failure", "execution_failure", "timeout"
report.result.verdicts           # ["ACCEPT", "DROP"] - what reduce_verdicts() returns
report.result.oracle             # readiness / liveness canary: observed, missed, not_reached
report.result.teardown_complete  # False if teardown failed or left resources behind
report.measurement_valid         # completed, cleaned up, every control and capture sound
report.write("artefacts/experiment.json")  # atomic, sorted keys

It never raises for a failed run. Rule, setup, oracle, execution and teardown errors are recorded with the stage they happened in, so a broken instrument, a timeout and an incomplete cleanup each have their own outcome. Cancellation still propagates.

The sections separate what is reproducible from what is specific to one run:

Section Contents Same on a re-run? input The request, with SHA-256 of the ruleset and of the request Yes environment NSE, Python, dependency, kernel and tool versions Yes, on the same host result Outcome, oracle status, verdicts per stimulus, errors by stage, residual resources, positive controls Yes, for a deterministic ruleset observations Trace and canary events, canary attempts, injection times, managed processes with verified identity, captures No: kernel trace ids differ run Test and ownership ids, namespace and interface names, timestamps, seconds per stage No

The report states what NSE measured, not what you expected: comparing the verdicts is your test's job, as the CLI does.

docs.title: Linking captures and positive controls
docs.text:
Captures and positive controls happen around the pipeline, so attach them afterwards. attach() returns a copy, hashes the files the captures wrote into report.artifacts, and lets them count towards measurement_valid:

from nse.models.experiment_report import PositiveControl

report = report.attach(
    captures=[await asserter.stop_report()],
    controls=[PositiveControl(name="probe seen with the ruleset flushed", passed=probe_seen)],
)
assert report.measurement_valid, report.result

docs.title: In pytest
docs.text:
import os

import pytest

from nse.cli.runner import collect_oracle_errors, reduce_verdicts
from nse.core.netns_controller import NetnsController
from nse.core.pipeline import run_test_pipeline
from nse.models.test_request import PacketSpec, TestRequest

pytestmark = [
    pytest.mark.asyncio,
    pytest.mark.skipif(os.geteuid() != 0, reason="NSE needs root for netns and kernel tracing"),
]

async def test_ssh_is_blocked(my_ruleset: str) -> None:
    request = TestRequest(
        rules=my_ruleset,
        packets=[PacketSpec(protocol="tcp", dst_port=22)],
    )
    events = await run_test_pipeline(request=request, controller=NetnsController())

    assert not collect_oracle_errors(events)
    assert reduce_verdicts(events) == ["DROP"]

docs.title: Streaming events as they arrive
docs.text:
Pass a queue to consume events live — useful for progress output on a long suite:

queue: asyncio.Queue = asyncio.Queue()
task = asyncio.create_task(run_test_pipeline(request=request, queue=queue))

while True:
    evt = await queue.get()
    if evt is None:  # sentinel: monitoring ended
        break
    print(evt.type, evt.trace_id, evt.verdict)

events = await task

The queue receives canary events too, since it is a raw feed; the list returned by the coroutine is the filtered one.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
Every timing knob is an environment variable, so you rarely need to touch code. See CLI reference. The two that matter most for slow machines and CI runners:

Variable Effect NSE_CANARY_ATTEMPTS Raise it if readiness canaries fail on a loaded runner. NSE_TRACE_IDLE_TIMEOUT Raise it if traces arrive slowly under heavy load.

Do not work around a failing canary by ignoring the error. A canary that never arrives means the engine could not see the kernel; whatever it would have reported about your ruleset would have been fiction.

docs.title: Running programs inside the namespace
docs.text:
NetnsController.create_namespace() yields a sandbox whose exec_argv() runs a program inside the namespace with exactly the arguments you pass:

async with controller.create_namespace("nse_app") as ns:
    result = await ns.exec_argv(["python3", "-c", "print('ciao mondo')"])
    assert result.stdout == b"ciao mondo\n"

Each list element reaches the process as one argument: spaces, quotes, empty strings, Unicode and shell metacharacters such as $HOME, * or ; are passed literally, because no shell and no splitting is involved. A bare string, a non-str element, an empty program name or an argument containing NUL is rejected with TypeError/ValueError before anything starts.

The older exec(command) is kept unchanged for existing callers. It splits the string on whitespace with str.split() and does not use a shell, so exec('python3 -c "print(1)"') passes the quote characters to Python and fails. Prefer exec_argv() for anything but the simplest commands.

Both methods return subprocess.CompletedProcess[bytes] whose args include the namespace prefix, and raise subprocess.CalledProcessError, with stdout and stderr attached, on a non-zero exit. Cancelling the call kills and reaps the process it started. The process runs with NSE's privileges: entering a network namespace changes the visible network, not the user. For a different identity, a timeout or a long-running program, use the managed processes below.

docs.title: Managed processes: identity, timeouts, process trees
docs.text:
start_process() starts a program and returns a handle; run_process() runs one to completion:

from nse import ProcessIdentity

nobody = ProcessIdentity(uid=65534, gid=65534, capabilities={"net_bind_service"})

async with controller.create_namespace("nse_app") as ns:
    # A server that must bind port 80 without being root.
    server = await ns.start_process(["/usr/sbin/my-server", "--port", "80"], identity=nobody)
    await server.wait_for_output(b"listening", timeout=10)  # explicit readiness
    assert server.identity.uids == (65534, 65534, 65534, 65534)

    # A client with a deadline: on timeout it is stopped and the result says so.
    result = await ns.run_process(["curl", "-sf", "http://[fd00:1::2]/"], timeout=5)
    assert result.ok, (result.termination, result.stderr)
# Leaving the block stops the server, its children and anything else still in the namespace.

Identity. ProcessIdentity sets the UID, GID, supplementary groups and capabilities. Every field defaults to "unchanged", so without it the program runs as NSE does. A non-root uid requires an explicit gid, and changing either clears the supplementary groups unless you list them. capabilities is exactly the set the process keeps (effective, permitted, ambient and bounding); it also works for root, for example to run root with net_raw only.

NSE enters the namespace with its own privileges and applies the identity afterwards with setpriv (util-linux; minimal images such as Fedora's util-linux-core lack it, and the error then names the package). Before the program starts, it reads the identity the kernel reports for that very process (same PID) and compares it with the request:

  • If anything differs, IdentityError is raised and the program never runs; there is no fallback to root.
  • If setpriv itself refuses, for example a capability the kernel does not know, the start fails with ProcessStartError.

The verified identity is in process.identity and in the result.

Output. stdin is /dev/null. stdout and stderr are captured by default, up to max_output_bytes each (1 MiB); the rest is counted in stdout_dropped / stderr_dropped, not kept. Pass "discard", or a path to write a new file instead: it is created with mode 0600, since output may hold secrets, and an existing file is never overwritten.

Ending a process.

  • wait(timeout) returns a ProcessResult with termination set to "exited", "timeout", "cancelled" or "terminated", plus the exit status (negative for a signal), the output and the identity.
  • On a timeout, on cancellation, or when you call terminate(grace), the process and its whole process group get SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after grace seconds.
  • result.check() raises CalledProcessError unless the process exited with 0.

The boundary. Each managed process leads its own process group. A descendant that leaves the group (setsid, a daemon that double-forks) is still in the network namespace. That namespace is the boundary NSE enforces: before it is deleted, at the end of the block or by crash recovery, every process in it is stopped, managed or not.

Processes are identified by namespace membership through a pidfd, so a recycled PID is never signalled, and recovery needs no record of PIDs. The one thing outside the boundary is a process that moves itself to another network namespace, which needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN. A dropped identity rules that out.

docs.title: The host endpoint and the host's firewall
docs.text:
By default the host end of the veth pair, ext_iface with host_ip, is in the namespace NSE runs in. Traffic from the sandbox to host_ip is then local input for that namespace and crosses its firewall. On Fedora, for example, firewalld puts the new vhr-* interface in the default zone, which accepts almost nothing. A server listening on host_ip never receives the request, and a test reads the silence as the rules under test blocking it.

NSE reads the host's nftables ruleset once per process and logs a warning when an input hook may filter that traffic: a drop policy, or a drop/reject reached unconditionally. It cannot tell which port a test uses, so it only warns. Rules loaded with iptables-legacy are not visible to it.

To take the host's firewall out of the path, pass isolated_host=True. The host end then goes into a namespace of its own, nsh_<name>, created and removed with the sandbox:

from nse import PCAPAsserter

async with controller.create_namespace("nse_app", isolated_host=True) as ns:
    # The host endpoint is a sandbox too: run the server where host_ip lives.
    server = await ns.host.start_process(["python3", "echo_server.py", "10.0.1.1", "9999"])
    await server.wait_for_output(b"bound", timeout=10)

    # Capture on the host end, in its namespace.
    asserter = PCAPAsserter(iface=ns.ext_iface, netns=ns.ext_netns)
    await asserter.start()
    result = await ns.run_process(["python3", "client.py", "10.0.1.1", "9999"], timeout=5)
    report = await asserter.stop_report()
  • ns.ext_netns is the namespace holding ext_iface: None by default, nsh_<name> when isolated.
  • ns.host is the host end as a sandbox. It has the same exec_argv(), start_process(), run_process() and inject_packet(). Its ext_iface is the sandbox's peer_iface, and the reverse, so ns.host.inject_packet() sends from the sandbox towards the host end.
  • ns.inject_packet() sends from inside nsh_<name>.
  • No host route is involved, so host_ip may overlap a subnet the host already routes. The preflight check for overlapping routes is skipped.
  • Processes on both ends are stopped when the block exits.

docs.title: Asserting that nothing left the interface
docs.text:
The trace oracle answers what did the ruleset decide. It cannot answer what reached the wire, which is the question behind a zero-leak claim: a packet that matches no rule at all produces no verdict to inspect. PCAPAsserter covers that half.

from nse import PCAPAsserter

asserter = PCAPAsserter(iface="veth-host")
await asserter.start()  # returns once the kernel socket is filtering and bound
# ... drive the stimulus: no sleep needed before it ...
leaked = await asserter.stop()
assert not leaked, f"{len(leaked)} frame(s) escaped: {leaked}"

The interface is looked up in the namespace NSE runs in. For one in another namespace, pass netns=, for example PCAPAsserter(iface=ns.ext_iface, netns=ns.ext_netns). Only the capture thread enters that namespace; the rest of the process stays where it is, and the report records it in netns.

docs.title: Readiness and failures
docs.text:
await start() returns only when the packet socket exists, carries its BPF filter and is bound to the interface. From that moment every matching packet is queued for the capture, so the stimulus may follow immediately; the asyncio.sleep() that older code put after start() is no longer needed. stop() drains whatever the kernel has already queued before closing, so a packet that reached the interface before stop() is not lost. A packet still in flight (for example, queued in another namespace) is not yet on the interface: wait for an observable effect of the stimulus, such as its arrival at a receiver, rather than a fixed delay.

start() raises CaptureStartError when the capture cannot be armed. Its reason is interface_missing, filter_invalid, permission_denied, backend_unavailable (libpcap missing), backend_error, timeout (see the optional timeout argument) or cancelled, and no thread or socket is left behind. A filter that does not compile is always an error. Scapy before 2.6 would log it and capture unfiltered; NSE compiles the filter itself first.

stop() still returns list[Packet], but raises CaptureError when the instrument was not healthy: the backend crashed (for example, the interface was deleted), the loop did not stop in time, or start had failed. An empty list now only ever means a working capture saw nothing. Calling stop() before start(), or start() twice, raises CaptureStateError. A capture is single use; stop() and stop_report() may be called repeatedly and in any order.

docs.title: The capture report
docs.text:
stop_report() stops the capture (once) and returns a CaptureReport instead of raising:

report = await asserter.stop_report()
report.instrument_healthy   # armed, ran until asked to stop, no backend error
report.window_complete      # True / False / None (unknown: counters unavailable)
report.termination          # "stopped", "limit_reached", "start_failed", ...
report.kernel_drops         # PACKET_STATISTICS drops, or None - never a guessed 0
report.effective_filter     # the BPF expression actually attached
report.model_dump_json()    # for CI artefacts

The report separates three questions. Instrument health says whether the capture worked. Window completeness says whether every matching packet between readiness and stop was read: the kernel's drop counter is zero and nothing remained unread. When the counters are unavailable this is None, not True. Evidence sufficiency is not in the report at all. A healthy, complete capture of an empty interface still does not prove that your stimulus took that path, which is why the positive control below is still required.

Beacons close part of that gap: await asserter.mark("label") sends a frame the capture must see, and a missing one makes the window incomplete. The report also gives the link type, the snaplen and, with PCAPAsserter(required_bytes=...), whether the snaplen is sufficient.

docs.title: Long captures with bounded memory
docs.text:
By default every captured packet is kept in memory and returned by stop(), exactly as before. For a capture that runs for minutes or sees heavy traffic, write it to a file instead and keep only counters in memory:

from nse import CaptureLimits, PCAPAsserter

asserter = PCAPAsserter(
    iface="veth-host",
    output="artefacts/leak-check.pcap",  # a new file: an existing one is never overwritten
    limits=CaptureLimits(max_duration=300, max_file_bytes=200_000_000),
)
await asserter.start()
# ... a long stimulus ...
report = await asserter.stop_report()

assert report.instrument_healthy, report.errors
assert report.window_complete is True, report       # nothing dropped, nothing cut off
assert report.packets_observed == 0, report.artifacts  # the leak assertion: on the counter

With output= the capture thread writes each packet to the PCAP file as it reads it. The file header is on disk once start() returns, the file is flushed whenever the capture is idle for a second, and it stays readable by tcpdump, Wireshark or scapy.utils.rdpcap even when it is cut short. Memory holds only a sample, which is empty unless you declare one with max_stored_packets or max_stored_bytes. stop() then returns that sample, so in file mode assert on the report, never on the list: assert not await asserter.stop() would pass even if packets leaked.

Every limit is optional, and reaching one is listed in report.limits_reached:

Limit When it is reached window_complete max_packets The capture ends itself after reading that many packets; later ones are not read. termination is limit_reached. False max_duration The capture ends itself that many seconds after readiness, after draining what was already queued. termination is limit_reached. False max_file_bytes File mode only. The first packet that would grow the file past the size, and every packet after it, is counted but not written: the file is a prefix of the capture. artifact_complete is False. False max_stored_packets Later packets are counted (and written, in file mode) but not kept in memory. False in memory mode; unaffected in file mode, where the file is the record max_stored_bytes Same, counted in bytes of packet data. As above

A capture ended by a limit is still a healthy instrument: stop() does not raise, but it logs a warning and the report says the window is incomplete. A file that cannot be written is a different matter. A full disk, or a write, flush or close error, appears in report.errors, makes the instrument unhealthy, and stop() raises CaptureError. The packets keep being counted, and the partial file is listed in report.artifacts with artifact_complete=False.

There is no queue between the socket and the file: the thread that reads the socket also writes the file. A writer that cannot keep up therefore fills the kernel socket buffer, and the kernel counts what it then drops (kernel_drops, window_complete=False). A writer that hangs (for example on a stalled network filesystem) makes stop() end with termination="stop_timeout". Neither case grows memory, and neither can produce a report that claims a complete capture.

The counters come from two places. packets_observed and bytes_observed are what NSE read from the socket. kernel_packets and kernel_drops are the kernel's PACKET_STATISTICS since readiness: every packet that passed the BPF filter, and the ones dropped because the buffer was full. packets_written and bytes_written describe the file. If the file is incomplete, it may hold fewer packets than were handed to it.

docs.title: Always pair it with a positive control
docs.text: A sniffer that never attached and a firewall that blocks everything both return an empty list. The assertion above distinguishes them only if you have shown, in the same run, that the instrument can see the packet you are looking for: flush the ruleset, send the same stimulus, and require it to be captured before you trust the empty capture that follows. Without that, the test passes hardest when it is most broken.

docs.title: The default filter, and when to replace it
docs.text:
DEFAULT_FILTER excludes ARP and ICMPv6 types 133-137 - Neighbour Discovery, whose hop limit of 255 means it cannot reach a remote observer. Everything else is captured, including ICMPv6 echo to a globally routable address.

A filter argument is combined with the default. Pass replace_default_filter=True to use yours alone:

# Combined: DEFAULT_FILTER and your expression.
PCAPAsserter(iface="veth-host", filter="ip6")

# Yours alone - you are now responsible for the noise.
PCAPAsserter(iface="veth-host", filter="ip6", replace_default_filter=True)

The escape hatch exists because the filter is compiled into BPF and evaluated in the kernel. A packet it excludes never reaches userspace, so a caller cannot compensate downstream by filtering the returned list - there is nothing in it to filter. Until 2.1.2 the default read not arp and not icmp6 and silently discarded routable ICMPv6 for exactly that reason; see issue #14.

docs.title: How-To: Observing a Stimulus
docs.text:
A test about a firewall is usually a test about an absence: "this packet did not leave". An absence has many causes, and most of them are the instrument failing, not the firewall working. nse.observe() runs a stimulus with a capture armed and, optionally, a receiver listening, and reports four facts separately:

Fact Source True False None (unknown) sent the sending process the send call succeeded it did not never on_wire the capture the probe's packet was seen a complete, healthy capture did not see it the capture was incomplete or unhealthy and did not see it received the receiver's log the receiver logged the probe a complete log does not have it no receiver, or an incomplete log without it reply_on_wire the capture a reply was seen as for on_wire as for on_wire

None is the instrument saying it cannot vouch for the absence. A test must never read it as False: assert not seen.on_wire passes on None, so assert seen.on_wire is False.

docs.title: A worked example: blocked, and provably so
docs.text:
from nse import NetnsController, ProcessIdentity, receivers, stimuli
from nse.core.rule_engine import RuleEngine

DROP_NOBODY = """
table inet egress {
    chain out {
        type filter hook output priority 0; policy accept;
        meta skuid 65534 drop
    }
}
"""

async def test_nobody_cannot_reach_the_host() -> None:
    controller = NetnsController()
    async with controller.create_namespace("nse_obs", isolated_host=True) as ns:
        RuleEngine().load(DROP_NOBODY, ns.name)
        probe = stimuli.tcp_round_trip("10.0.1.1", 9999)

        async with await receivers.tcp_echo("10.0.1.1", 9999).start(ns.host) as echo:
            # Positive control: another user, the same path, the same instruments.
            control = await stimuli.observe(
                ns, probe, identity=ProcessIdentity(uid=1000, gid=1000), receiver=echo
            )
            blocked = await stimuli.observe(
                ns, probe, identity=ProcessIdentity(uid=65534, gid=65534), receiver=echo
            )

    assert control.on_wire is True, control.describe()
    assert control.received is True, control.describe()
    assert control.reply_on_wire is True, control.describe()

    assert blocked.on_wire is False, blocked.describe()    # not None: a complete window
    assert blocked.received is False, blocked.describe()   # not None: a complete log
    assert blocked.contradictions() == [], blocked.describe()

By default the capture is on the sandbox's host end (ns.ext_iface in ns.ext_netns). Pass iface=, netns= or capture_filter= to change it, and settle= for how long to keep capturing after the stimulus returns.

Here the SYN from UID 65534 never leaves, and connect() simply times out (no_reply at connect). The process cannot tell a dropped SYN from a silent server; the capture can, and only because its window was complete.

docs.title: Contradictions: a blind instrument fails visibly
docs.text:
Some combinations of facts cannot all be true. contradictions() lists them, and describe() appends each as CONTRADICTION: ...:

  • received, but not on the wire: the capture is blind to the path the traffic took (a wrong interface, a filter that excludes it). Its silence about anything else proves nothing.
  • answered, but no reply on the wire: the capture is blind to the return path.
  • on the wire, but the process reported could_not_run or a refused send: the probe's own report is wrong.

A refused connect or receive with the packet on the wire is not a contradiction: a TCP RST or an ICMP error follows a packet that did leave.

A capture on the wrong interface is still a complete window that saw nothing, so on its own it reports on_wire=False. A receiver, or a canary that must be seen (below), is what exposes it. NSE's own tests run exactly that case with a filter that excludes the probe.

docs.title: A canary in the same window
docs.text:
A positive control in its own capture proves the instrument worked a moment ago, not that it was still working during the stimulus. Pass canary=: a stimulus the rules under test let through, sent after the stimulus inside the same capture window.

seen = await stimuli.observe(
    ns,
    stimuli.tcp_connect("10.0.1.1", 8080),
    identity=nobody,
    canary=stimuli.udp("10.0.1.1", 7777),
    canary_identity=allowed,          # default: the stimulus's identity
)
assert seen.canary.on_wire is True, seen.describe()
assert seen.on_wire is False, seen.describe()

Unless the canary was seen on the wire, no absence is False: on_wire, reply_on_wire and the other unseen facts become None, and describe() says canary: NOT seen. A capture that stopped reading, or never watched the traffic's link, cannot vouch for a silence it did not observe. The beacons prove the same thing at the link level, and the two combine.

docs.title: Several stimuli in one window
docs.text:
observe_window() runs several stimuli in order, then the optional canary, inside one capture, and gives each stimulus its own Observation:

window = await stimuli.observe_window(
    ns,
    [stimuli.udp("192.0.2.53", 53), stimuli.tcp_connect("192.0.2.80", 80)],
    identity=nobody,
    canary=stimuli.udp("10.0.1.1", 7777),
    canary_identity=allowed,
)
assert window.conclusive, window.describe()   # healthy, complete, canary seen, no contradiction
dns, web = window                              # one Observation per stimulus, in order
assert dns.on_wire is False
assert web.on_wire is False

window.vouched is the capture's part (healthy, complete, canary seen), window.contradictions() gathers every observation's contradictions, and window.packets holds the whole capture. Each stimulus is matched by its own probe ID (or, for a bare SYN, its source port), so neither the canary nor another stimulus can stand in for it.

To drive the capture yourself instead, find each result's packets with requests_in() and replies_in():

asserter = PCAPAsserter(iface=ns.ext_iface, netns=ns.ext_netns)
await asserter.start()
probe = await stimuli.udp("192.0.2.53", 53).run(ns, identity=nobody)
control = await stimuli.udp("10.0.1.1", 9999).run(ns, identity=allowed)
report = await asserter.stop_report()
packets = await asserter.stop()

assert report.window_complete is True, report
assert stimuli.requests_in(control, packets), "the window was not open after the probe"
assert not stimuli.requests_in(probe, packets), "the probe left"

docs.title: After a NAT
docs.text:
By default a request must go to the stimulus's own destination address and port. A DNAT or a redirect rewrites both, so the probe is no longer recognised. With a receiver at the new destination this shows up as a contradiction: received, but not on the wire.

Pass nat=True to observe(), observe_window(), requests_in(), replies_in() or correlate(). The destination is then not compared: a request counts wherever it goes, as long as it leaves from the probe's own source and carries its probe ID (or, for a bare SYN, leaves from its bound port). A reply counts from whatever source answered, as long as it is addressed to the probe. Read where the probe really went from the packets:

seen = await stimuli.observe(ns, stimuli.udp_round_trip("10.0.1.1", 5353), identity=nobody,
                             receiver=echo_on_9999, nat=True)
assert seen.on_wire is True
assert {pkt[UDP].dport for pkt in seen.requests} == {9999}   # redirected

A NAT that rewrites the source port of a bare SYN still hides it, since that port is the SYN's only identity.

docs.title: How-To: Controlled Receivers
docs.text:
A capture says a packet was on the wire. It does not say the packet arrived: the destination's input path can still drop it, and a reply can only come from something that received the request. A controlled receiver is a known server that logs every arrival, with its probe ID, before answering it.

Run receivers on the host endpoint of an isolated sandbox (create_namespace(..., isolated_host=True), then ns.host). There, no firewall on the machine running NSE sits between the sandbox and the receiver. See the host endpoint.

docs.title: A worked example: a DNS rule that must not answer for blocked users
docs.text:
from nse import NetnsController, ProcessIdentity, receivers, stimuli

async def test_the_resolver_sees_the_query() -> None:
    controller = NetnsController()
    async with controller.create_namespace("nse_dns", isolated_host=True) as ns:
        server = receivers.dns("10.0.1.1", a=("192.0.2.10",))
        async with await server.start(ns.host) as resolver:
            result = await stimuli.dns_query("10.0.1.1").run(
                ns, identity=ProcessIdentity(uid=1000, gid=1000)
            )
            log = resolver.log()

    assert result.outcome == "answered", result.describe()
    assert result.dns.addresses == ("192.0.2.10",)
    assert log.complete, log.problems
    [receipt] = log.matching(result)            # the resolver got this very query
    assert receipt.source == result.source      # from the address the probe used

start() returns only once every socket is bound: the receiver says so explicitly, so there is no sleep and no race with the first stimulus. If it cannot bind (an address the namespace does not have, a port in use) start() raises ReceiverStartError with the reason instead of returning a server that will never answer.

docs.title: The receivers
docs.text:
Constructor Listens on Answers udp_echo(address, port=0) UDP the datagram, unchanged tcp_echo(address, port=0, idle_timeout=5.0) TCP every segment, unchanged dns(address, port=53, a=..., aaaa=..., mode="answer") UDP and TCP on one port fixed A/AAAA records stun(address, port=3478) UDP a Binding success with XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS

Port 0 picks a free port; receiver.port says which.

The DNS receiver's mode decides what happens to a query:

mode Response answer the configured a or aaaa records (NOERROR, empty for other types) servfail SERVFAIL refused REFUSED drop nothing: the query is logged and not answered

drop is the negative control for a client's timeout handling: the query arrived (received) and no reply was sent.

docs.title: The receipt log
docs.text:
receiver.log() is a snapshot while the receiver runs; await receiver.stop() (or leaving the async with block) gives the final one. Each Receipt has:

  • seq: a counter from 1, so a gap is visible;
  • probe_id: extracted from the data, or None for data without one;
  • source and destination (Endpoints), family, transport;
  • kind: datagram, connection (a TCP accept) or data;
  • monotonic and wall: when it arrived;
  • size, data (the first 512 bytes) and response (what the receiver did: echo, answer, servfail, drop, binding and so on).

Find receipts with for_probe(probe_id), from_source(endpoint) or matching(result). matching uses the probe ID, or the source port for a bare SYN, which carries no data.

docs.title: An incomplete log proves nothing
docs.text:
log.complete is False, with the reasons in log.problems, when:

  • a sequence number is missing or a line cannot be read;
  • the receiver's output exceeded the limit and was cut;
  • the receiver exited on its own instead of being stopped;
  • the final line was cut off.

A receipt found in an incomplete log still counts. An absence in an incomplete log is not a finding: observe() reports it as "received: unknown", never as "not received".

docs.title: How-To: Sending Traffic as a User (Stimuli)
docs.text:
A firewall usually decides on locally generated traffic in its output hook, by UID, GID or cgroup. Packet injection cannot test that: an injected frame has no owning socket. The traffic has to come from a real socket in a process running as the identity under test.

nse.stimuli does that. Each stimulus is a small standard-library program run inside the sandbox through run_process(), with an optional ProcessIdentity. It opens a socket, sends, optionally waits for a reply, and reports what happened as a typed StimulusResult.

docs.title: A worked example: a per-user egress rule
docs.text:
The sandbox drops everything UID 65534 sends to port 53, and nothing else. The test proves both halves: the rule stops that user, and spares another user.

import errno

from nse import NetnsController, ProcessIdentity, stimuli
from nse.core.rule_engine import RuleEngine

RULES = """
table inet egress {
    chain out {
        type filter hook output priority 0; policy accept;
        meta skuid 65534 udp dport 53 drop
    }
}
"""

NOBODY = ProcessIdentity(uid=65534, gid=65534)
USER = ProcessIdentity(uid=1000, gid=1000)

async def test_only_nobody_is_blocked() -> None:
    controller = NetnsController()
    async with controller.create_namespace("nse_egress") as ns:
        RuleEngine().load(RULES, ns.name)
        query = stimuli.udp("10.0.1.1", 53)

        blocked = await query.run(ns, identity=NOBODY)
        allowed = await query.run(ns, identity=USER)

    assert blocked.outcome == "refused", blocked.describe()
    assert blocked.stage == "send"
    assert blocked.errno == errno.EPERM          # the firewall, not a broken probe
    assert allowed.outcome == "sent", allowed.describe()

describe() gives one line for an assertion message, for example udp 10.0.1.1:53 probe 3f9c…: refused at send (EPERM: Operation not permitted).

docs.title: The outcomes are never folded together
docs.text:
outcome Meaning Typical stage sent The send call succeeded. Nothing was waited for. none answered A reply came back (or, for tcp_connect, the handshake completed). none no_reply The probe waited and nothing came: only for stimuli that wait. receive, connect refused A socket call failed. errno and error say how. connect, send, receive could_not_run No packet can have been produced. reason says why. launch, socket, bind, output

could_not_run is never a pass. It covers an interpreter that is missing, an identity that cannot be applied, a socket that cannot be created (a raw socket without CAP_NET_RAW), a source port that cannot be bound, and a program that crashed or printed no report. A containment test that accepts it would pass with no traffic at all.

refused and no_reply are kept apart for the same reason. A rejected datagram comes back as ECONNREFUSED on receive (refused); a datagram that was dropped further on is a timeout (no_reply).

docs.title: What the process cannot tell you
docs.text: A UDP datagram dropped by an output rule fails send() with EPERM. A TCP SYN dropped the same way does not fail connect(): the kernel retransmits it until the stimulus gives up, so the result is no_reply at connect. Only a capture can say the SYN never left. Use observe() whenever the absence of a packet is the claim.

docs.title: The stimuli
docs.text:
Every constructor takes the destination as an IP literal; the family (IPv4 or IPv6) follows from it.

Constructor Sends Waits for a reply udp(host, port) one datagram no udp_round_trip(host, port, timeout=2.0) one datagram yes tcp_connect(host, port, timeout=1.0) a bare SYN (a handshake, no data) the handshake tcp_round_trip(host, port, timeout=2.0) a connection and a payload yes icmp_echo(host, timeout=None, socket="raw") an ICMP or ICMPv6 echo request when timeout is set dns_query(server, transport="udp", qtype="A") a query for a unique name, over UDP or TCP yes quic_initial(host, port=443) a 1200-byte datagram shaped like a QUIC Initial when timeout is set stun_binding(host, port=3478) a STUN Binding Request yes

Stimulus.with_reply(timeout) turns any of them into one that waits (or, with None, one that does not).

  • DNS: the result's dns holds the parsed answer: rcode_name, addresses, qname. A reply that cannot be parsed is still answered, with the parse error in error.
  • STUN: mapped_address is the source address and port the server saw, which is what a NAT or a proxy rewrites.
  • ICMP: socket="raw" needs CAP_NET_RAW. Running as root has it; a non-root identity needs capabilities={"net_raw"}. socket="dgram" uses a ping socket instead, which works without the capability only for groups in net.ipv4.ping_group_range.

docs.title: Probe IDs and the 5-tuple
docs.text:
Every run gets a new probe ID (24 hex digits) carried in the packet itself: in the payload for UDP, TCP and ICMP, in the query name (nse-<id>.nse.test) for DNS, in the transaction ID for STUN and in the connection ID for QUIC. A bare SYN has no payload, so it binds a distinct source port from its own counter, and that port identifies it. The result records the source address and port (source) the kernel chose, for every kind that has one.

This is what lets a capture or a receiver say "this packet is that probe" rather than "a packet like it went by".

docs.title: Requirements: setpriv
docs.text:
A stimulus with an identity is launched through setpriv, from util-linux. Like every binary NSE runs as root, it is looked up only in trusted system directories, never in $PATH. Minimal images may not have it: Fedora's util-linux-core has nsenter but not setpriv. Install util-linux.

Without it, every stimulus run as another identity is could_not_run at launch, with the reason naming the package, and StimulusStream.start() raises StreamStartError. A stimulus without an identity does not need it.

docs.title: The interpreter
docs.text: The programs need only the Python standard library. By default they run with the interpreter running NSE, resolved through any virtualenv symlink, with -I -S so nothing from the caller's environment is imported. Pass python="/usr/bin/python3" to run() when the sandbox user cannot read that interpreter.

docs.title: How-To: Traffic Through a Window of Time (Streams)
docs.text:
A single probe says what happened at one instant. A rule reload, a service restart or a teardown takes a window of time, and the question is what happened to the traffic throughout it: did anything slip through while the old rules were gone and the new ones not yet in place?

A StimulusStream sends the same stimulus once per period from a process inside the sandbox, numbering every attempt. correlate() joins the stream's log with a capture and a receiver's log and says, for each sequence number, how far it got. It also says whether the stream covered the whole window: a stream that paused says nothing about the pause.

docs.title: A worked example: a rule loaded mid-stream
docs.text:
The stream runs as UID 65534 toward a UDP echo receiver. Half-way through, a rule that drops that user's traffic is loaded. Every attempt before the load must be received, every attempt after it refused, and the window must be conclusive on both sides.

import asyncio
import time

from nse import NetnsController, PCAPAsserter, ProcessIdentity, receivers, stimuli
from nse.core.rule_engine import RuleEngine
from nse.streams import StimulusStream, correlate

DROP_NOBODY = """
table inet egress {
    chain out {
        type filter hook output priority 0; policy accept;
        meta skuid 65534 udp dport 9999 drop
    }
}
"""

async def test_the_drop_takes_effect_without_a_leak() -> None:
    controller = NetnsController()
    async with controller.create_namespace("nse_reload", isolated_host=True) as ns:
        async with await receivers.udp_echo("10.0.1.1", 9999).start(ns.host) as echo:
            capture = PCAPAsserter(iface=ns.ext_iface, netns=ns.ext_netns)
            await capture.start()
            await capture.mark("start")

            stream = StimulusStream(stimuli.udp("10.0.1.1", 9999), period=0.02)
            async with await stream.start(ns, identity=ProcessIdentity(uid=65534, gid=65534)) as running:
                await asyncio.sleep(0.3)
                load_started = time.monotonic()
                await asyncio.to_thread(RuleEngine().load, DROP_NOBODY, ns.name)
                load_done = time.monotonic()
                await asyncio.sleep(0.3)

            await capture.mark("end")
            packets = await capture.stop()
            report = await capture.stop_report()
            receipts = await echo.stop()

    joined = correlate(running.log(), packets, receipts, capture=report)
    assert joined.conclusive, joined.describe()

    before = joined.between(joined.window_start, load_started)
    after = joined.between(load_done, joined.window_end)
    assert set(before.counts()) == {"received"}, before.describe()
    assert set(after.counts()) == {"refused"}, after.describe()

Leaving the async with block stops the stream and waits for the attempts in flight. The start and end beacons make the capture prove it was reading across the whole window.

Attempts that start while the rule is being loaded can go either way. They are in joined but in neither slice, which is why the slices are taken at load_started and load_done.

docs.title: What became of each attempt
docs.text:
Status Meaning not_sent The attempt could_not_run (no packet can exist), or its record is missing from the log refused A socket call failed (refused, with its errno) and the capture did not see the packet sent_not_seen It left the socket, and the capture does not have it on_wire The capture has it; the receiver does not (or there is no receiver) received The receiver logged it

The strongest evidence wins: a packet the capture saw is on_wire whatever the process reported. Each Fate also keeps the attempt's StimulusResult and the two facts it rests on, on_wire and received. As in observe(), each is True, False (a complete instrument did not see it) or None (it cannot say). fate.conclusive is True only when the status rests on facts the instruments can vouch for.

joined.counts(), joined.with_status("on_wire", "received") and joined.describe() are there for assertions and their messages.

docs.title: When the window is inconclusive
docs.text:
joined.conclusive is False, and joined.problems or joined.gaps say why, whenever an instrument cannot vouch for the window:

  • The stream paused. No attempt that could run started for longer than max_gap_periods periods (default 3). The process was not scheduled, the machine stalled, or too many attempts were in flight. Each pause is a Gap with its start, end and the sequence numbers around it.
  • Attempts could not run. An attempt that could_not_run produced no packet, so it covers no time. A stream of them is one long gap, and a stream with no attempt that could run tested nothing.
  • The stream's log is incomplete. Sequence numbers are missing, a line was cut or unreadable, the output limit was hit, or the stream did not report its end. A log read while the stream is still running is not final either.
  • The capture cannot vouch for an absence. There was no capture, no report, or the report is not healthy and complete, for instance with a missing beacon or kernel drops. Packets that were seen still count.
  • The receiver's log is incomplete.
  • The instruments contradict each other. The receiver logged what the capture missed, or the capture saw what the process says it never sent.

between(start, end) keeps these problems and adds gaps at the edges: a slice the stream did not cover from end to end is not conclusive either.

docs.title: The schedule
docs.text:
StimulusStream(stimulus, period=0.02, count=None, duration=None, max_in_flight=256)
  • Timing. Attempts are scheduled from the stream's start on a fixed grid. Each one runs in its own thread with its own socket, so an attempt that waits (a reply timeout, a SYN to a dropped port) does not delay the next.
  • Slots that cannot be used. A slot is skipped when max_in_flight attempts are already running, or when the process was not scheduled in time. Skipped slots are never made up with a burst: they show as a gap.
  • Ending. count or duration end the stream by itself; wait for it with await running.wait(). Without them it runs until await running.stop(), or until the async with block ends.
  • Probe IDs. Every attempt carries its own probe ID: a 16-digit stream ID followed by the sequence number in 8 hex digits. A bare-SYN stream binds a distinct source port per attempt instead, counting up from a random base and skipping any port that is busy, so no two attempts share one.
  • Times. StreamAttempt.started_monotonic is CLOCK_MONOTONIC, the clock time.monotonic() reads, so it compares directly with times the test takes.

stream.start() raises StreamStartError if the program does not say it started within ready_timeout seconds. A stream whose attempts all fail has started; each failure is in its log.

docs.title: NAT
docs.text: When a DNAT or redirect rewrites the stream's destination, pass correlate(..., nat=True) to recognise each attempt by its probe ID wherever it went. See Observing a Stimulus.

docs.title: How-To: Tracing a Process's Own Traffic
docs.text: nft monitor trace names the rule that decided a packet's fate, which a capture cannot. NSE's trace set-up enables tracing in a prerouting chain, because its oracle injects packets from outside.
